draft.title: The Battle of Leuctra
card: In 371 BC a Theban army led by Epaminondas defeated Sparta at Leuctra, a village in Boeotia. Sparta had long been seen as unbeatable on land.
Epaminondas made the left wing of his phalanx very deep, about 50 men, and put his best troops there. He faced it against the Spartan right, where the Spartan king Cleombrotus stood.
The Spartans lost about 1000 men, including Cleombrotus and several hundred Spartiates, the full citizens. Sparta had few citizens left, so such losses were hard to replace.
Sparta never recovered its old power. Soon after, Thebes led an invasion of Laconia, and Messenia, which Sparta had ruled for centuries, was freed from Spartan control.
draft.remember: Leuctra broke the Spartan army's name for being unbeatable, and without it Sparta lost Messenia.

a.q: Why were the Spartan losses at Leuctra so damaging to Sparta?
opts: Few citizens were left, so the losses were hard to replace
The king survived and fled, so his rule lost all authority
Most of the fleet was sunk, so Sparta lost its trade routes
The helots won the vote, so the citizens lost their power
a.why: Sparta relied on a small body of full citizens, so hundreds killed could not be made up quickly. The king did not survive: Cleombrotus died in the battle.
a.clue: Think about how many full citizens Sparta had.

b.q: Which result followed soon after Thebes defeated Sparta at Leuctra?
opts: Messenia was freed from Spartan control
Thebes took over Sparta's place as ruler of Messenia
Sparta won back its power in a later battle at Leuctra
Athens replaced Sparta as leader of the Peloponnese
b.why: After Leuctra, Thebes led an invasion of Laconia and Messenia was freed from Sparta. Thebes did not take over Messenia: the result was freedom from Spartan rule, not rule by Thebes.
b.clue: Which land had Sparta ruled for centuries?

a.best: Few citizens were left, so the losses were hard to replace

b.best: Messenia was freed from Spartan control
